#1893. Exeter City v Crawley Town: We now feel we can compete, says Blackwell

Crawley extended their unbeaten run in the league under Blackwell to four games with a 0-0 draw at home to title contenders Barnet in midweek – and Blackwell now believes that his side are “competitive” – not only on the eye but also according to the data.

The former Sheffield United manager said: “The data shows that we're very competitive now with sprints, decelerations, accelerations, high-speed runs. We're now coming at the top half of the table with that so it just shows that we've been improving all over.”

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

From a defensive point of view the past two games have shown a rejuvenated back-line – helped by the recent additions of Ben Heneghan and Josh Flint, which have made the Reds look a lot more resolute and solid.

Exeter are currently one spot below the play-off places sitting in 8th place on 23 points. The Grecians have the best defensive record in the league having only conceded 10 goals but Blackwell is not fazed by that.

He has communicated as much to his players: “It doesn't matter whether they're the top or the bottom, we feel now that we can compete with people, and that's all I wanted to do, make us competitive. Then hopefully Lady Luck smiles on you on the day and you can get some good results.”

Blackwell was pleased that more players have stepped up to the mark to give him more confidence in choices.

He said: “We talk about how any team wants to be competitive from 1-22 really, and know that if you lose a player, that someone can seamlessly step in. What was pleasing was that we made some changes, shifted it around a little bit, and then whoever we brought in did a good job, so that gives me more power.”

With the Reds involved in a lunchtime kick-off, Blackwell was asked whether that makes a difference to the way they approach the game.

He replied: “I think it's something that I've been used to now for the last 15 years, you know, being in a Championship or the Premier League and abroad in Poland is exactly the same.

“You don't know whether you're playing a Friday, a Saturday, a Sunday or a Monday, they're the four days that you normally play.

“You don't know whether you're going to be at 12 o'clock, 2pm, 4pm, 8pm – so it's now it's just normal for players; it certainly has been for me. So nothing different, whatever the time is, we'll prepare as if it were a 3pm kick-off or a 1pm kick-off. Preparation is the same.”

#1892. Eastbourne Town in turmoil – who will take over Macdonald and can team get out of trouble?

The club’s decision to go for a change at the top has caused a huge amount of upset – with many fans saying it is a shocking decision and a number of Macdonald’s squad deciding to follow him out of the door. And it is the way the decision appears to have been handled that has caused the most anger.

As the week unfolded, Town – who are second from bottom of the Isthmian South East division after only two wins in 19 games – appointed club stalwart Dave Winterton as interim manager, with senior player Arron Hopkinson assisting him, and asked fans to get behind him.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

And they put out an advert inviting applicants for the job, with talk of them wanting to take the whole club – not just the men’s first team – forward as one.

Macdonald’s right-hand man Ben Davis has gone in the wake of the sacking and so, reportedly, have long-serving Adam Davidson and at least five players.

Macdonald gave an exclusive interview to the Eastbourne Herald and sussexworld.co.uk in which he said he had been told eight days before he was sacked that his job was ‘bomb-proof’ all the time the chairman was in place.

He also said he had learned the club had decided they wanted a change of manager on November 16 – and only after two more games, training and two more siginings did they tell him. Macdonald told us he was asked if would resign, but refused.

You can read our full interview with Macdonald, who has been at the helm since 2022, on pages 62 & 63. He finished it with these words: “You don’t often get the chance to manage the club from the town you grew up in and I’ve just committed over 10% of my life to it, so the next few days and weeks will just be reflecting on that and appreciating the opportunity that the club gave me four-and-a-half years ago, and the continued and consistent success we have given them in return.”

As for what happens next, Winterton isinterim manager and the Town committee have asked fans to get behind him as he guides the squad through what will be a tricky period.

The immediate aim is to try to get out of the Isthmian SE danger zone, and that starts with a visit to Erith Town tomorrow, followed by a home Sussex derby with Broadbridge Heath a week later.

Those won’t be easy games with a number of Macdonald’s players announcing they also left – including James Waters, who had only rejoined the club a day before the manager was ousted.

Meanwhile the club – who gave ‘sincere thanks’ to Macdonald in their statement revealing he was leaving – are inviting applicants for the vacancy. They said: “We are looking for an individual who shares our ambition, understands the importance of building a strong club culture and is passionate about developing players, creating opportunities and delivering success both on and off the pitch.

"At Eastbourne Town, we believe the First Team should be an important part of a wider football development pathway. We want to create an environment where young players can see a realistic route from youth football through U18 and U23 football and ultimately into the first team.”

#1891. Crawley Town boss: Post-match celebrations are for players – not for me

Since taking over, the Reds are unbeaten in four in the league, and despite dropping out of both cup competitions in the space of three days, there has been a mentality shift in the players – and the fans have seen that the players are giving their all.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Speaking in his pre-Exeter press conference, Blackwell said one or two fans asked him why he didn’t go and thank the support: “I thank the fans all the time, but after the game, it’s important that the players get the credit, not the manager.

“That’s not my job. My job is to try to prepare the team, and the players go out and give everything. If they do that, that’s what the fans want. They don’t want me walking up and down the pitch clapping and whatever. Get on, do your job Blackwell, do your job. And if that’s the case, the players are doing well.”

He added: “It’s not my style. I enjoy them enjoying it and I enjoy that the fans enjoy it. I’ve had a great career, managing big clubs and been a long way in big competitions, been all over the world, and I’ve never wanted the adulation.

“I just enjoy other people having it and seeing my players get that and the fans enjoying it. Sending them home after a week’s work, seeing the players give everything. That’s what they want. If we can keep doing that, I think we keep them on-side.”

Talking about the bond between players and fans, Blackwell said “I want the players to take the credit because the bond is between the players and the fans, and that’s the bond.

"As an ex-player, I knew there was a great bond between me and the fans. I’d hate to think that the manager walked up and started taking my thunder after having a man of the match performance and he walks up and takes all the credit. No, I want the players to have the credit.”

#1890. PSV Eindhoven vs. Go Ahead Eagles - prediction, team news, lineups

By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 14:12

Looking to move on from their midweek Champions League collapse against Real Madrid, PSV Eindhoven return to the bread and butter of Eredivisie football on Saturday.

The defending champions welcome Go Ahead Eagles to the Philips Stadion in gameweek 14, seeking a response to their humbling experience in the Spanish capital as they chase a fourth consecutive top-flight victory.

An Ivan Perisic goal made things interesting at the Bernabeu in midweek, but a Jude Bellingham-inspired second-half performance saw Jose Mourinho's Los Blancos run riot and eventually claim a 5-1 victory over PSV.

That loss, the Dutch giants' third in five European matches, leaves them 30th in the 36-team league-phase standings and their top-eight prospects looking increasingly remote.

However, Peter Bosz's men remain in contention for the qualification playoffs, with 24th-placed Villarreal just two points ahead of the reigning Eredivisie champions.

The Farmers will undoubtedly welcome a return to home comforts on Saturday as they seek to regain winning momentum after their chastening experience in the Spanish capital.

League football has brought greater encouragement, particularly in recent weeks, with three consecutive victories following a run of one win in four matches between late September and late October.

Scoring at least four goals in each of their victories over Willem II (7-0), Cambuur (6-2) and NEC (4-1) suggests a return to their free-scoring best, boding well for this weekend's visit from Go Ahead Eagles.

The Deventer outfit travel to Eindhoven in indifferent form, with a 1-0 away victory over SBV Excelsior coming between defeats to Cambuur and Fortuna Sittard.

Particularly notable has been the attacking decline of Joseph Oosting's men, who have scored just once across their last three league matches after averaging 2.3 goals per game over the opening 10 gameweeks.

While that sample remains too small for firm conclusions, the Pride of the IJssel's dip cannot be dismissed ahead of their trip to the Philips Stadion, where Kowet claimed a stunning 2-1 KNVB Beker semi-final victory in February 2025 en route to lifting their first domestic cup.

Paul Simonis was in charge for that historic success as Go Ahead Eagles secured their first victory in Eindhoven for 57 years, and they now seek a first Eredivisie win at PSV since 1968.

That will be easier said than done, however, as their historical struggles and recent scoring decline leave them vulnerable against hosts still reeling from their Santiago Bernabeu beatdown.

Mauro Junior (groin), Sami Ouaissa (muscle), Adamo Nagalo, Alassane Plea and Jerdy Schouten (ACL) remain unavailable for PSV; however, Ricardo Pepi should feature in some capacity after remaining on the bench in Madrid.

No player has scored more Eredivisie goals than Sven Mijnans, with the versatile attacking midfielder registering nine strikes and three assists in the top flight.

Guus Til is likely to lead the attack despite Pepi's availability, while Ruben van Bommel offers a dual threat after contributing five goals and three assists.

Soren Tengstedt shares Mijnans's position atop the league's scoring charts, with no player outscoring the Kowet forward this season.

Stefan Ingi Sigurdarson (four goals, one assist) and Mathis Suray (three goals, four assists) also possess match-winning quality that Oosting will hope comes to the fore at the Philips Stadion.

Go Ahead Eagles remain without Pim Saathof (ACL), while Evert Linthorst and Dean James will be assessed closer to kick-off.

Kovar; Dest, Geertruida, Obispo, Kostic; Sano, Fernandez; Perisic, Mijnans, Van Bommel; Til

Go Ahead Eagles possible starting lineup:

Cillessen; Sampsted, Dirksen, Kramer, Baeten; Meulensteen, Rahmouni; Tengstedt, Edvardsen, Suray; Sigurdarson

PSV's collapse in Madrid exposed their limitations in Europe, but scoring 17 goals across their last three Eredivisie victories underlines the different challenge they present domestically.

Go Ahead Eagles have managed just one goal in their last three league matches, and the hosts have our backing to deliver a convincing response at the Philips Stadion.

#1889. OLIVER HOLT: Man United ARE in a relegation battle - anybody who denies it is deluding themselves - and Mauricio Pochettino is already showing signs of cracking under pressure

Published: 07:54 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 10:31 EST, 23 November 2026

Early on in On the Road, somewhere between Chicago and Denver, Jack Kerouac described the journey his main character was taking and some of the trepidation that came with each new horizon. ‘I was halfway across America,’ he wrote, ‘at the dividing line between the East of my youth and the West of my future.’

Late on Sunday afternoon, as winter’s grey light turned to darkness on Merseyside and a bitter wind blew in off the Irish Sea, Manchester United’s new boss, Mauricio Pochettino, freshly arrived from Cincinnati, Ohio, arms folded grimly and tightly across his chest, stood on the touchline at Anfield and realised the full extent of what he had just got himself into.

Sure, the United job was too big to turn down. However far the club has fallen, it still has that lure. It still has the name, even if the name is now just one of those building facades on a film set.

There is the name and then there is the nothingness that is concealed beyond the name. There is the mismanaged, mistreated void that United has become.

And now United need to find out which version of Pochettino they have purchased. Because he is at a dividing line, too. Do they have the Pochettino who blazed a trail across the football landscape with Espanyol, Southampton and Spurs, although he did not win trophies at any of those destinations?

Or do they have the Pochettino whose reputation gradually became becalmed at Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USA national team? They better hope they can restart something in him because this is the biggest and the hardest job Pochettino has ever had and it will take a Herculean effort just to survive.

Do Man United have the Mauricio Pochettino who blazed a trail with Espanyol, Southampton and Spurs? Or do they have the Pochettino whose reputation has fluctuated since?

That is what this season is about now for these fallen, ruined giants. It is about survival. Nothing more. If Pochettino did not realise it before, he will have realised it during that calamitous 4-0 defeat at Anfield: United are in a relegation battle and anyone who denies that is deluding themselves.

That is just pride talking. The remnants of what pride remains at United, anyway.

Maybe it hasn’t quite seemed real until now. Just like the prospect of Leicester City winning the Premier League didn’t start to feel real until around Christmas of 2015-16. United going down would be up there with Leicester winning the title in terms of seismic events in the modern English game. It’s time to start taking relegation seriously.

If you take the blinkers off for just a second, if you banish the muscle memory that tells you United are too successful and too rich to get sucked down into the Championship, then you have to accept that all the ingredients are there for United to get relegated. Take that name away and what’s left?

What’s left is a team that last won a Premier League game on August 30. What’s left is a team that has won one game all season. What’s left is a team that has conceded 34 goals across all competitions, more than any other team in Europe's top five leagues. What’s left is a team that has eight points from its first 11 league games.

Just for context, the Spurs side that spent most of last season haunted by the prospect of relegation, had 18 points at this stage of that campaign. If you still think the rabble currently representing the club are too good to go down, I think you are deluding yourself.

Yes, United played more than 80 minutes of the game against Liverpool with 10 men and, yes, the decision to send off Leny Yoro for his challenge on Alexander Isak was harsh. But the dismissal was also a fig-leaf for Pochettino and United. It was convenient. It was a disguise for what lay beneath.

United also brought it on themselves. Pochettino made one big selection decision before the game when he picked Matthijs de Ligt ahead of Harry Maguire. It was what former bosses in the English game might have described as a ‘big rick’. It was a terrible misjudgment.

Maybe the sending off of Leny Yoro was harsh. But United brought it on themselves

Matthijs de Ligt (right) was bullied by Alexander Isak at Anfield. Pochettino's decision to play the Dutchman was a terrible misjudgment

De Ligt’s first action was to watch a long ball from Ronald Araujo sail over his head, gazing at it with a mix of horror and wonder, as you might if you were watching the trajectory of an alien spaceship. Yoro was not quick enough to read De Ligt’s discomfort and so the horror ensued.

It was Pochettino’s first game and it is impossible to judge him yet but it is possible to say this was a bad start.

There were even a couple of worrying signs in his post-match press conference when the bonhomie and the relaxed demeanour that are among his great strengths deserted him.

When he was asked about United being in the relegation zone, he snapped that it was a ‘cheap’ question because he had only just arrived at the club. He said he saw fight in his players, which few others had seen. He blamed everything on the sending off of Yoro, even though it was his selection of De Ligt that had led to it.

A few alarm bells started to ring. Only faintly and only in the distance but they were ringing nonetheless. Pochettino has had big jobs before but he has never had a job as big as Manchester United where the scrutiny and the expectation and the judgment is relentless and unforgiving.

Pochettino has dealt with Daniel Levy at Spurs, which may not have been an easy relationship, but he has never dealt with a clown-show like the one that Jim Ratcliffe has put in place at Old Trafford.

United is rotten. Everyone can see that. Off the pitch, the club is at war with its own fans. The club gives every impression of trying to move on its most loyal supporters so that it can replace them with tourists and day-trippers who will spend more on tickets and in the club superstore and at the food stands.

‘The way you treat us is a disgrace,’ that banner in the Stretford End said a few weeks ago, and that is how the fans feel. They are more loyal than United deserve but their patience with their owners ran out a long time ago. Pochettino has a disaffected fanbase to deal with as well.

United is rotten on the pitch and it is rotten off the pitch. It feels as if the club is being slowly poisoned in plain sight. It feels as if it is getting weaker and weaker and weaker. And when Brentford arrive at Old Trafford next week, they will smell blood. Every club that comes to Old Trafford now smells blood.

Harry Maguire looks dejected at full-time on Sunday. United is rotten on the pitch and it is rotten off the pitch. It feels as if the club is being slowly poisoned in plain sight

Still think they’re too good to go down? Who are they better than in this league? Hull City? United don’t have the spirit of Hull City. They don’t have the togetherness. They don’t have the pride.

Hull got battered by Brighton on Sunday afternoon and still won 2-0. United could never have done that. United have already lost to Hull and Brighton this season, too.

So, yes, United are in a relegation fight. They’re one off the bottom of the league in the last week of November. Of course, they’re in a relegation fight. It’s on their new boss to get them out of it.

If Pochettino is on the wrong side of the dividing line of his career, if the best part of his journey is behind him, United are in big, big trouble.

#1888. I watched Celtic leave it late in Portugal and noted gamble pay off, emotional homecoming and serious issue

Unconvincing Celtic kept their Europa League qualification hopes alive with a hard-fought and historic 2-1 victory over Portuguese second-tier side Torreense.

Martin O’Neill’s men took an early lead through a Javi Vazquez own goal after nine minutes, but Dany Jean restored parity for the hosts before half-time in Leiria.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The visitors struggled to find a breakthrough after the interval, until substitute Camilo Duran rose unmarked to head home James Forrest’s cross in the 84th minute.

The late winner secured a second consecutive victory in the competition for Celtic, moving them on to six points from five matches and up to 25th in the league-phase standings after keeping their hopes of reaching the knockout stages alive.

It was also the Scottish champions’ victory win on Portuguese soil since 2003.

Lewis Anderson watched the action unfold for The Scotsman and picks out his four main takeaways from the game.

Celtic may have made unnecessarily hard work of beating a Portuguese second division outfit currently sitting 13th in their league, but Martin O’Neill will care little about the aesthetics after securing three precious points.

Although Celtic enjoyed plenty of possession after the interval, their use of the ball was frequently pedestrian, with too many passes going sideways or backwards rather than putting Torreense under meaningful pressure. There were spells when Celtic appeared destined to settle for a frustrating draw, but ultimately they have given themselves a genuine opportunity to reach the play-off round and, at this stage of their European campaign, that is what matters most.

Once again, Camilo Duran proved to be the difference-maker. O’Neill's decision to keep the in-form striker in reserve paid dividends, with the substitute delivering the decisive moment when Celtic needed a spark. The Colombian’s back-post header from fellow replacement James Forrest’s pinpoint delivery was precisely the injection of quality that had been missing for much of the evening.

When the ball arrived at his feet, his first touch was outstanding, allowing him to open his body and switch the play. He then demonstrated the instincts of a natural goal scorer, occupying defenders before finding the space to deliver the decisive finish. Duran may have had only 12 touches, but the one that mattered most was emphatic. He is becoming Celtic's go-to man in crucial moments, and delivered once more when it counted.

Although Jota did not manage to get his name on the scoresheet or provide an assist, his performance in Portugal offered plenty of telltale signs that he is rediscovering the devastating form that once made him such an exciting attacking presence for Celtic. The winger looked particularly at home on his return to familiar surroundings, relishing the chance to perform in front of friends and family after an arduous period on the sidelines.

Making his first European appearance since Celtic’s Champions League disappointment against Bayern Munich in February 2025, the 27-year-old showed few signs of rustiness despite two injury-disrupted seasons. He was a constant menace to Torreense down the left flank, using his pace, close control and willingness to take on defenders to cause problems throughout his time on the pitch.

His influence was particularly evident during the opening period, creating two opportunities, testing the goalkeeper twice and delivering a succession of enticing crosses that deserved more decisive finishing from his team-mates. One such delivery contributed to Celtic's opening goal, when Vazquez inadvertently turned the ball into his own net.

Given the length of his absence and the physical demands of returning to elite-level football, there had been understandable questions over whether Jota could recapture the explosive qualities that previously made him a favourite among the Celtic support. His latest display provided a really encouraging response. There is still work to do before he reaches his previous heights, but the signs are increasingly promising.

This success has breathed fresh life into Celtic's European campaign, but O’Neill will be under no illusions that there is considerable scope for improvement if his side are to make further progress. Individual contributions may have rescued the evening in Portugal, yet they should not disguise some worrying collective shortcomings, particularly the vulnerability of the defence and the lack of composure when chances presented themselves in the final third.

The format offers Celtic a route into the knockout stages, with the top eight in the league phase advancing automatically to the last 16, while those finishing between ninth and 24th must negotiate a two-legged play-off. There remains little margin for error, though, with three fixtures remaining. Celtic still have Omonoia, Marseille and current league-phase leaders Union Saint-Gilloise to negotiate, and will almost certainly require further points if they are to extend their European journey.

There is, however, reason for optimism. The win over Torreense means Celtic have now recorded successive wins in a major European competition for the first time since defeating Ferencvaros home and away during the 2021-22 group stage of this tournament. It is a positive milestone for O’Neill's side and another indication that, despite their problems, Celtic are beginning to build some momentum at a crucial stage.

Torreense may have been unfancied on paper, but they demonstrated they were no pushovers and gave Celtic a considerably sterner test than their second-tier status might have suggested. The Portuguese outfit were organised, and disciplined, refusing to be overawed by the occasion or the gulf in resources between the two clubs.

João Nuno’s side pressed aggressively, competed well for second balls and showed enough attacking ambition to expose some of Celtic's defensive vulnerabilities. Their equaliser was reward for an approach that refused to crumble after falling behind, while their resistance after the interval threatened to frustrate the visitors further.

Celtic's superior individual quality eventually told, but Torreense deserve credit for making them dig deep for the result. This was no routine European assignment. For all the criticism Celtic will face over aspects of their performance, Torreense should not be dismissed as cannon fodder. They showed spirit and sufficient quality to suggest their lowly league position told only part of the story.

#1886. Real Madrid vs. Alaves: Head-to-head record and past meetings ahead of La Liga clash

By Matt Law | 26 Nov 2026 14:18, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 14:18

Real Madrid will be aiming to continue their excellent run of form when they welcome Alaves to Bernabeu on Saturday evening.

Los Blancos will enter the league fixture off the back of a thumping 5-1 victory over PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League.

Jose Mourinho's side have now won each of their last 10 matches in all competitions, including their last six fixtures in Spain's top flight.

Real Madrid beat Celta Vigo 2-1 in the league last time out, and they currently sit second in the La Liga table, three points behind the leaders Barcelona.

Alaves, meanwhile, have been one of the success stories in La Liga this season, picking up 16 points from 13 matches, which has left them in ninth spot in the table.

Here, Sports Mole rounds up the head-to-head record and looks at the previous meetings between the two teams ahead of their clash in the Spanish capital.

Real Madrid have tackled Alaves on 46 occasions throughout history, and unsurprisingly, the Madrid giants lead the overall head-to-head record with 38 wins to Alaves five, while there have only ever been three draws between the two teams.

Karim Benzema is the all-time leading goalscorer in this fixture, having scored nine times against Alaves during his time at Real Madrid.

Real Madrid are on 121 goals against Alaves, conceding just 34, and Los Blancos are on a nine-game winning run against the Basque side.

That said, Alaves do have a recent famous win over Real Madrid to their name, having recorded a 2-1 victory when the two teams locked horns at Bernabeu in November 2020, thanks to goals from Lucas Perez and Joselu.

Alaves have beaten Real Madrid only twice since 2000, though, while there has not been a draw between the two sides since October 2001.

Two of Alaves' five wins over Los Blancos have actually come at the Bernabeu, also triumphing 1-0 in the famous stadium back in 2000.

In La Liga, the teams have met on 40 occasions, with Real Madrid winning 34 times to Alaves' four, drawing twice in the process.

#1884. ‘Curious’ Derek McInnes used Jamestown Analytics to rate Rangers signing while Hearts manager

Derek McInnes has revealed that he used Jamestown Analytics to rate Rangers' signing of Ryan Naderi while manager of Hearts last season.

Hearts gained access to Jamestown's treasure trove of player recruitment data in 2024 after selling a stake in the club to the man who formed the company, Brighton chairman Tony Bloom.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

While used primarily to source signings for their own squad, Hearts are also able to access information on signings made by their Premiership rivals.

McInnes admitted that he ran Naderi through the system and was left hoping that Rangers would not sign the Czech striker as he was identified as a good signing for the Ibrox club.

He explained: "Last January, obviously, when we first seen that Rangers were linked with Naderi, like everyone else, I would say to [Hearts sporting director] Graeme Jones, 'How do they rate him?'

"Because you're always curious. It's just the way it is. It's brilliant when you see other teams round about you signing a player that's not rated. That's the way it was. It's just natural.

"But no, he was someone that I think was well known to them. I think Brugge had an interest in Ryan, and I think USG potentially had an interest in him as well. But the kind of money, the fee, it just kind of went away for them, I think.

"But we were told that he was a good player before I'd even set eyes on him. The feeling was that he was somebody that could help Rangers and make them better. So when I'd seen a lot of the comings and goings, it was on, it was off, it was off, on again, I was kind of hoping that it would fall through, being the Hearts manager. But when I'd seen they'd signed him, I knew that Rangers had strengthened. And I think Rangers did strengthen well in January last year.

"So that was the first we kind of looked a wee bit more at him but, again, you just do it as an opposition manager, looking at him. It's only when you get to work with people on a daily basis that you get to see them."

Naderi initially struggled to live up to his £4.75million transfer tag after joining Rangers in January from German third tier side Hansa Rostock.

However, the 23-year-old has emerged as a talismanic figure this season, scoring 10 goals in his last 20 games and providing the focal point in attack following injuries to Youssef Chermiti and Lawrence Shankland.

"I had a good conversation with Ryan when I first came in the door about what we felt this season could look like for him," McInnes said. "Because it's not always easy for a young player settling in January and they're in the middle of a race, but to try and really establish himself this season.

"I think he stood up brilliantly to a couple of the senior injuries, to other injuries throughout, to Youssef and Lawrence. He's had to be the guy and he's led the line brilliantly. I love the goals he scores. I love his work rate anyway. But it's nice that people don't just see him as a grafter now and a worker. He's actually got good intelligence.

"All top strikers have intelligence to be in the right place at the right time and it's symptomatic of some of the goals he scores, following things in, just always believing there might just be something there for me.

"I love having a striker that has the ability to score those types of goals. But he leads the line well, gets us up the pitch and works ever so hard, as you know. He's done well. He should feel pleased. I think the fact that he's got capped as well, he's taken a real step on from that. I think he's taken a lot of confidence from that.

"However he gets his confidence, whether it's scoring goals, whether it's staying fit, being a big part of the team, whether it's getting recognised at international level, we all want it to continue."
